content: 1. Patients undergoing tuberculosis (TB) treatment or healthcare providers may be offered additional interventions to improve treatment adherence. These interventions are complementary and not mutually exclusive. They include: a) The use of tracers and/or digital medication monitors, which is a conditional recommendation based on very low certainty of evidence. b) Providing material support to individuals with TB, which is a conditional recommendation supported by moderate certainty of evidence. c) Offering psychological support to patients, which is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence. d) Educating healthcare staff, which is a conditional recommendation with low certainty of evidence. 2. For individuals receiving TB treatment, the following treatment administration options may be considered: a) Community-based or home-based directly observed treatment is recommended over health facility-based or unsupervised treatment. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence. b) Treatment administered by trained lay providers or healthcare workers is recommended over treatment administered by family members or unsupervised treatment. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. c) Video-observed treatment (VOT) may replace directly observed treatment if video communication technology is available and can be appropriately organized and managed by healthcare providers and patients. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 3. Individuals with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) should primarily receive ambulatory care rather than care models based on hospitalization. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 4. A decentralized model of care is recommended over a centralized model for individuals undergoing MDR-TB treatment. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 5. Household contacts, particularly infants, children, and individuals living with HIV, are at the highest risk of TB infection. All individuals with TB should be interviewed, and their close contacts traced and assessed according to recommended practices. People living with HIV should be screened for TB disease at every visit to healthcare facilities. 6. TB preventive treatment (TPT) involves administering one or more TB medications to prevent the development of active TB disease. TPT is provided to individuals infected with TB bacteria or those exposed to it and at higher risk of developing TB disease compared to the general population. TPT is a critical public health measure to protect individuals and communities from TB. WHO recommends TPT for people living with HIV, childhood contacts, household contacts, and other high-risk groups, as these populations derive the greatest benefit from preventive treatment. 7. Systematic screening of household contacts and people living with HIV should be prioritized to identify and promptly treat those with active TB disease. People living with HIV should receive at least six months of isoniazid preventive treatment (IPT) without prior tuberculin skin testing, regardless of previous TB treatment, current antiretroviral therapy (ART), degree of immunosuppression, or pregnancy status. 8. For TB contacts, the choice of TPT depends on the drug resistance profile of the source case. Preventive treatment may also be considered for selected high-risk household contacts of individuals with MDR-TB based on individualized risk assessment and sound clinical justification. 9. People initiating anti-TNF treatment, undergoing dialysis, preparing for organ or hematological transplantation, or with silicosis should be systematically tested and treated for latent TB infection (LTBI). Systematic LTBI testing and treatment may also be considered for prisoners, healthcare workers, immigrants from high TB burden countries, homeless individuals, and people who use drugs. 10. Systematic LTBI testing and treatment are not recommended for people with diabetes, those who engage in harmful alcohol use, tobacco smokers, or underweight individuals unless they belong to other high-risk groups included in the above recommendations. 11. Either a tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) can be used to test for LTBI. TST measures the immune response intradermally, with induration measured after 48–72 hours. IGRA measures the immune response in a single blood sample, providing results within 24–48 hours. 12. Various TPT regimens are available depending on the drug resistance profile. These include six or nine months of daily isoniazid, a three-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a three-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. Alternative regimens include one month of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or four months of daily rifampicin alone. 13. In settings with high TB transmission, adults and adolescents living with HIV who have an unknown or positive LTBI test and are unlikely to have active TB disease should receive at least 36 months of daily IPT. This should be provided regardless of ART status, degree of immunosuppression, history of previous TB treatment, or pregnancy. 14. Children under 15 years of age are particularly vulnerable to TB infection and disease, making them a priority group for prevention, early detection, diagnosis, and treatment. Infants, children, and young adolescents who are HIV-positive or household TB contacts should be screened for active TB disease, and those without TB disease should start TPT. 15. Shorter TPT regimens are preferred for children, such as three months of daily isoniazid and rifampicin (3HR) for HIV-uninfected contacts and children living with HIV (CLHIV) on efavirenz-based ART regimens weighing up to 25 kg, or three months of weekly isoniazid and rifapentine (3HP) for older household contacts. Six months of daily isoniazid (6H) remains the most suitable option for CLHIV on other ART regimens. 16. Asymptomatic neonates born to mothers with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB should receive TPT after excluding TB disease and be regularly monitored to confirm the absence of TB. Neonates who remain asymptomatic and HIV-negative at the end of TPT should receive BCG vaccination using the normal infant dose. 17. BCG vaccination should be included in national immunization programs and administered to all infants as soon as possible after birth. 18. WHO guidelines recommend systematic TB prevention and care for individuals under 15 years of age, emphasizing the importance of BCG vaccination, TPT, and early detection and treatment of TB in this vulnerable population.
